scope: Curated reference summaries for an MND genetics pre-test counselling research prototype.

entries.title: Evidence-based consensus guidelines for ALS genetic testing and counseling
entries.publisher: Annals of Clinical and Translational Neurology
entries.summary: The consensus group recommends offering genetic testing to all people with ALS, with genetic counselling and education. Its minimum panel recommendations include C9ORF72, SOD1, FUS, and TARDBP, plus other genes with definitive evidence. C9ORF72 repeat-expansion analysis requires an appropriate assay and is not equivalent to ordinary sequence analysis.

entries.title: Pre-test genetic counselling recommendations in ALS
entries.publisher: Annals of Clinical and Translational Neurology
entries.summary: Pre-test counselling should take place before testing. It should review a three-generation family history, explain genetic heterogeneity, inheritance and incomplete penetrance, discuss possible positive, negative and uncertain outcomes, and consider personal, family, psychological and practical effects. Testing remains the person's choice.

entries.title: Post-test genetic counselling recommendations in ALS
entries.publisher: Annals of Clinical and Translational Neurology
entries.summary: Post-test counselling is recommended for all result types. A pathogenic result may explain a genetic contribution but often cannot predict an individual's exact course. A negative result does not exclude every genetic contribution. A variant of uncertain significance should not be treated as a confirmed cause and may be reclassified as evidence changes. Relatives should receive specialist counselling before predictive testing.

entries.title: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Overview
entries.summary: GeneReviews provides a clinician-reviewed overview of ALS, genetic causes, inheritance patterns, testing approaches and family implications. A person can have a genetic cause without an obvious family history because families may be small, diagnoses may differ, information may be unavailable, or a variant may have reduced penetrance or be new in that person.

entries.title: Inherited MND and genetic testing
entries.summary: This UK patient information resource explains inherited MND, why testing may be discussed, possible implications for relatives, and the role of specialist genetic counselling. It is suitable as a plain-language companion to a clinical appointment, but individual decisions and result interpretation belong with the neurology or genetics team.

entries.title: Frequently asked questions about genetic testing
entries.summary: This MND-specific FAQ addresses practical questions people commonly raise about genetic testing and family implications. Processes, eligibility and waiting times can vary by service, so local details should be checked with the person's clinical team.

entries.title: Inherited MND and genetic counselling
entries.summary: This UK information sheet describes how genetic counselling can help a person explore testing, possible results, family implications and their own preferences. Counselling supports an informed choice; it is not intended to direct a person toward or away from testing.

entries.title: Standards and guidelines for the interpretation of sequence variants
entries.publisher: American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics and Association for Molecular Pathology
entries.summary: This standard defines the widely used five-tier sequence-variant classification framework: pathogenic, likely pathogenic, uncertain significance, likely benign and benign. A VUS is an inconclusive finding and should not be presented as a confirmed diagnosis or used alone for predictive testing decisions.

entries.title: Motor neurone disease: assessment and management (NG42)
entries.publisher: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence
entries.summary: NICE NG42 covers assessment and multidisciplinary management of MND in the UK. It supports coordinated, person-centred information and care. It is a general MND care guideline rather than a substitute for specialist genetics guidance.

entries.title: Shared decision making (NG197)
entries.publisher: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence
entries.summary: NICE recommends making decisions collaboratively, discussing options and their benefits, risks and consequences, and supporting people to consider what matters to them. This is relevant to preference-sensitive choices such as genetic testing.
